drills.q: List the five stages of an ordered EDA process.
drills.a: 1) Grain and shape 2) per-column univariate checks (dtype, missingness, skew, cardinality) 3) relationships between features (Pearson and Spearman) 4) relationship to target (binned means, class balance) 5) leakage and imbalance hunt, done last.

drills.q: A feature has mean=520, median=310 on a transaction-amount column. What does this tell you and what should you check next?
drills.a: Mean > median indicates right skew (a long tail of large transactions). Check scipy.stats.skew() to quantify it, and if |skew| > 1, avoid z-score outlier detection on this column -- use IQR or modified z-score instead.

drills.q: You compute Pearson correlation between a feature and the target and get r=0.05. Is it safe to conclude the feature has no useful relationship to the target?
drills.a: No. Pearson only measures linear relationship strength. A monotonic-but-nonlinear relationship (e.g. y=x^3) or even a strong non-monotonic (U-shaped) relationship can produce a near-zero Pearson r. Check Spearman for monotonic relationships and a binned-mean plot for any shape.

drills.q: Your z-score outlier filter (threshold=3) on a right-skewed latency column flags almost nothing, yet you know from domain knowledge that some requests take absurdly long. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: The std is inflated by the distribution's own long tail, so genuinely large values no longer register as '3 std away' because the std baseline is already stretched by other tail values. Switch to IQR-based detection (Q1-1.5*IQR to Q3+1.5*IQR) or modified z-score using median/MAD, both robust to the skew.

drills.q: A feature 'discharge_disposition' includes the category 'transferred to hospice' and correlates at 0.4 with a hospital-readmission target. Is a 0.4 correlation low enough to rule out leakage?
drills.a: No. A moderate correlation doesn't rule out leakage -- a leak can be partial (encoding an intermediate variable or only some of the outcome) and still meaningfully inflate offline metrics without hitting a too-good-to-be-true threshold. The real test is whether this value could exist, in this form, at the moment the prediction needs to be made -- 'transferred to hospice' is recorded at essentially the same event that determines readmission status, which is a leakage red flag regardless of correlation magnitude.

drills.q: Design an EDA check that would catch a feature like days_since_last_payment being null only for accounts in good standing (a classic leakage pattern), beyond a simple correlation check.
drills.a: Group by the feature's missingness (df.groupby(feature.isna())[target].mean()) and check whether the target rate differs sharply between the missing and non-missing groups -- if missingness itself correlates strongly with the target, the feature's EXISTENCE pattern is leaking information, even if a raw correlation on the non-null values looks unremarkable.

drills.q: You have a 99.5%/0.5% imbalanced fraud dataset. List three specific things this changes about your EDA and evaluation plan, beyond 'don't use accuracy'.
drills.a: 1) Stratify train/test/CV splits or a fold can end up with too few positive examples, making its metric noise. 2) Reconsider what 'outlier' detection is even for -- IQR/z-score-flagged points might be the minority class's characteristic signature, not noise. 3) Prefer PR-AUC over even ROC-AUC, since ROC-AUC can also look deceptively good under extreme imbalance.

drills.q: Explain what Anscombe's Quartet demonstrates and derive the practical EDA rule that follows from it.
drills.a: Multiple datasets can share identical mean, variance, and Pearson correlation to several decimal places while looking completely different when plotted (one linear, one with an outlier driving the fit, one a clean curve, one two clusters). Rule: never trust a correlation number or summary statistic as a final verdict -- use it to triage which pairs deserve an actual scatterplot, then look at the plot before concluding anything.

drills.q: You need to EDA a 500-column, 50-million-row dataset but full profiling would take hours. Design a scaled-down approach, and name the risk you're accepting.
drills.a: Sample rows (compute cost scales with rows more than statistical precision does past a threshold), then use a cheap full-column pass (single tree model feature importances or per-column mutual information against target) to shortlist plausible predictors before running expensive O(p^2) pairwise correlation only on the shortlist. Risk accepted: a rare but genuinely important interaction living in a column outside the shortlist could be missed -- mitigate with the cheap full-pass importance step rather than relying purely on domain-knowledge shortlisting.

drills.q: A model trained and validated on a historical snapshot has excellent offline test AUC but degrades in production within weeks. Standard train/test evaluation didn't catch it. What EDA step would have?
drills.a: Comparing feature distributions between the training snapshot and current production data (e.g. via a sweetviz-style comparison report) -- a train/test split from the same historical snapshot can't detect that the world has moved on since collection. This is EDA applied to the pipeline over time, not just the static dataset.
